description: How recruitment posters, Owen's poetry and modern historians have reshaped how we read 1890-1918.
content_html:
Why Do Historians Interpret the Past Differently?

History is not simply a record of events — it is also a story about how we interpret those events, shaped by the sources available, the questions historians ask, the time at which they write, and the values they bring. The period 1890–1918 is especially rich in competing interpretations because it touches on questions that still matter: empire, sacrifice, gender, class and the nature of heroism. Understanding historiography is a key skill in examining this period.

Key Fact

A primary source is evidence produced at or close to the time being studied (a recruitment poster, a soldier’s letter, a census). A secondary interpretation is a historian’s analysis written after the fact. Both have value, but for different purposes.

Sources: Recruitment Posters and Their Utility

Government recruitment posters are one of the most widely used primary sources for 1914–1916. The most famous — Alfred Leete’s “Your Country Needs YOU” image of Kitchener — was produced in 1914. Others used emotional pressure: images of children asking their father what he did in the war, or women handing white feathers to men in civilian clothes.

To assess a source’s utility, a historian considers three things together: content (what does it actually show or say?), provenance (who produced it, when, why, and for what audience?) and contextual knowledge (what do we already know that helps us read its significance and limits?). A recruitment poster is highly useful as evidence of government propaganda methods — but tells us little about whether those appeals worked or what soldiers genuinely believed. It must be used alongside other evidence.

Wilfred Owen wrote most of his major poems between August 1917 and September 1918 at Craiglockhart hospital in Edinburgh, where he met Siegfried Sassoon. His poem Dulce et Decorum Est describes a gas attack in graphic detail and ends by challenging the “old lie” that it is sweet and proper to die for one’s country. Owen was killed on 4 November 1918 — one week before the armistice — aged 25.

As a primary source, Owen’s poetry is valuable for understanding the psychological impact of the Western Front on educated officers. However, it is limited as evidence of typical soldiers’ attitudes: Owen was an officer, a poet, and wrote at a specific moment of disillusionment. Millions of ordinary soldiers left no comparable record. Historians of the “revisionist” school argue that focusing on the war poets creates a distorted picture that exaggerates disillusionment across the army.

Interpretations of the First World War

Historians have disagreed profoundly about the First World War. The dominant view in the 1920s and 1930s — shaped by the anti-war literature of Sassoon, Owen, and Robert Graves — presented the war as needless slaughter managed by incompetent generals who sent men to their deaths from comfortable chateaux far from the front. This “lions led by donkeys” interpretation became embedded in popular culture through plays such as Oh, What a Lovely War! (1963).

From the 1960s onwards, professional historians began to challenge this picture. John Keegan pioneered “history from below,” focusing on the experience of ordinary soldiers rather than commanders’ strategies. His The Face of Battle (1976) examined what it was actually like to be at Agincourt, Waterloo or the Somme.

Niall Ferguson, in The Pity of War (1998), made several provocative arguments: that Britain’s entry into the war was not inevitable or necessary; that the German advance could have been allowed to proceed without Britain’s involvement; and that the human cost of the war was ultimately Britain’s own choice. Ferguson’s thesis was controversial because it reversed the standard account of German aggression as the war’s primary cause. Critics argued he underestimated the genuine threat German hegemony in Europe would have posed to British interests and democracy.

The interpretations differ for several reasons: Ferguson wrote in the post-Cold War 1990s when empire and military sacrifice were less unquestionable values; he had access to archival sources unavailable to earlier historians; and he was asking a counterfactual question (“what if Britain had stayed out?”) that conventional diplomatic historians had not prioritised. This illustrates the key principle: interpretations change because historians ask different questions and write from different contexts.

Feminist Historiography of the Suffrage Campaign

The history of women’s suffrage has also been interpreted in conflicting ways. For much of the twentieth century, the Suffragettes — the WSPU and the Pankhursts — dominated the popular narrative, celebrated as heroic militants. From the 1970s onwards, feminist historians began to recover the history of the constitutional Suffragists (NUWSS), arguing that Millicent Fawcett’s patient, legal campaigning was equally or more important to eventual success.

A further debate concerns why women won the vote in 1918: was it because of militant suffragette pressure, wartime service, or a combination of long-term constitutional pressure and changed political circumstances? The answer depends partly on how much weight historians give to short-term versus long-term causes — a classic second-order concept debate that mirrors the wider question of how historians explain change.

Key Fact

Interpretations differ because historians write at different times, ask different questions, use different sources, and are influenced by the values of their era. For the 1890–1918 period, the key debates are: was the First World War necessary? Were the generals competent? Did militancy or constitutional pressure win women the vote?
exam_tip_html: For the 10-mark ‘Compare Interpretations’ question, never just explain what each interpretation says — that is answering how they differ, not why. Focus on the reasons for the difference: the author’s purpose, the time of writing, the evidence used, and any personal or political perspective. For ‘Source Utility’ questions, always weigh content, provenance and contextual knowledge together — saying a source is biased does not make it useless.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Primary sources (recruitment posters, Owen’s poetry) are assessed for utility through content, provenance and contextual knowledge together. A biased source can still be useful evidence — of what the producer wanted people to believe.
  • Historians such as Keegan and Ferguson offer contrasting interpretations of the First World War based on the questions they asked, the time they wrote and the sources they used. Revisionist historians challenged the “lions led by donkeys” narrative from the 1960s onwards.
  • Interpretations change over time. The key question in the 10-mark exam question is always why interpretations differ, not just what they say.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of how historians have interpreted the First World War.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a developed point. Example: Some historians (such as those influenced by war poetry) have argued that the war was needlessly costly slaughter managed by incompetent generals (1), an interpretation sometimes summarised as 'lions led by donkeys' (1). Mastering: accurate feature with supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Wilfred Owen's war poetry as a historical source.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature examples: written at Craiglockhart hospital 1917-18 by a shell-shocked officer — making it valuable evidence of psychological impact; graphic anti-war imagery (Dulce et Decorum Est) challenges official propaganda — useful for understanding disillusionment; limited as evidence of typical soldiers' views since Owen was an educated officer not representative of all ranks. Mastering: two precise features with accurate detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why John Keegan's interpretation of the First World War differed from earlier interpretations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Keegan pioneered 'history from below' in The Face of Battle (1976), focusing on the experience of ordinary soldiers rather than commanders' strategies; earlier interpretations were shaped by the anti-war literature of the 1920s–30s (Sassoon, Owen, Graves) which reflected officer perspectives; Keegan used different source types and asked a different question — what was combat actually like for the men who fought? — giving a more grounded, less political picture. Secure (3–4): clear reason with development. Developing (1–2): simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why two historians might reach different interpretations of women's suffrage in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Historians ask different questions — one might focus on the short-term impact of WSPU militancy (arguing it forced the government's hand), while another might focus on long-term constitutional pressure (arguing the NUWSS's 20-year campaign created the political conditions); they might also be influenced by the values of the era in which they write — feminist historians from the 1970s recovered Fawcett's role that had been overlooked by earlier histories focused on dramatic Suffragette action. Secure (3–4): clear reason with development. Developing (1–2): simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Compare what the recruitment posters of 1914-1916 and Wilfred Owen's war poetry suggest about the First World War.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per source, comparing what each suggests. Recruitment posters: suggest the war was a patriotic duty, heroic and necessary; emphasise nation, family and obligation; produced by the government to encourage enlistment. Owen's poetry: suggests the war was brutal, psychologically damaging and based on a lie; produced by a disillusioned officer recovering from shell shock. The sources differ because they were produced by people with fundamentally different purposes and experiences — government propagandists versus a traumatised soldier-poet. Mastering: precise comparison with reference to both provenance and content.

practice_questions.text: 'Niall Ferguson's interpretation of Britain's entry into the First World War is more convincing than the traditional view.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Agree and disagree, substantiated, overall judgement. Agree: Ferguson's access to post-Cold War archives and his counterfactual approach reveals choices that earlier historians treated as inevitable; his critique of British decision-making is supported by evidence of how the cabinet debated entry in late July 1914. Disagree: the traditional view — that German aggression (invasion of Belgium, militarism, the Schlieffen Plan) made British entry necessary — is supported by the evidence of Germany's own planning; Ferguson underestimates the strategic threat a German-dominated Europe would have posed; most professional historians continue to see Britain's entry as justified by circumstances. Balanced judgement: Ferguson raised important questions but the traditional view remains more convincing on the primary evidence. Secure (7-9): argument both ways. Developing (4-6): limited. Emerging (1-3): one-sided.

knowledge_checks.q: What are the three elements historians must consider together when assessing the utility of a source?
options: Primary source, secondary source, and tertiary source

knowledge_checks.q: Which historian wrote The Pity of War (1998), controversially arguing that Britain need not have entered the First World War?
Wilfred Owen wrote most of his major war poems at _____ hospital in Edinburgh, where he met Siegfried Sassoon.
The study of how and why historical interpretations are produced and change over time is called _____.
Match each historian or source to its key feature:
right: Soldier-poet whose Dulce et Decorum Est challenged the glorification of war
Historian who pioneered 'history from below' in The Face of Battle (1976)

flashcard_questions.q: What three things must a historian weigh together to assess a source's utility?

flashcard_questions.a: British soldier-poet (1893-1918) who wrote graphic anti-war poems including Dulce et Decorum Est.

flashcard_questions.q: When was Owen killed, and how close to the end of the war?
flashcard_questions.a: 4 November 1918 — one week before the armistice.
The study of how historical interpretations are produced, why they differ, and how they change over time.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the 'lions led by donkeys' interpretation of the First World War?
flashcard_questions.a: The view that brave soldiers were sent to needless deaths by incompetent generals.

flashcard_questions.q: Who wrote The Face of Battle (1976) and what was his key contribution?
flashcard_questions.a: John Keegan — he pioneered 'history from below', focusing on ordinary soldiers' experience.

flashcard_questions.q: What was Niall Ferguson's controversial argument in The Pity of War (1998)?
flashcard_questions.a: That Britain need not have entered the First World War in 1914 — the entry was a choice, not an inevitability.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do interpretations of the suffrage campaign differ between earlier and feminist historians?
flashcard_questions.a: Feminist historians from the 1970s recovered Fawcett and the NUWSS; earlier historians focused mainly on the dramatic Suffragette militants.

flashcard_questions.q: What makes a recruitment poster useful as a primary source?
flashcard_questions.a: It is strong evidence of government propaganda methods and the appeals used to motivate volunteers.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a limitation of using Owen's poetry as evidence about the typical soldier's experience?
flashcard_questions.a: Owen was an educated officer — his perspective was not representative of millions of ordinary enlisted men.

glossary_terms.definition: The study of how historical interpretations are produced, why they differ, and how they change over time as new evidence emerges or historians ask new questions.
Visual posters produced by the government to encourage men to volunteer for military service, combining patriotic imagery with direct emotional appeals.
British soldier and poet (1893-1918) who wrote graphic anti-war poetry at Craiglockhart hospital in 1917-18; killed one week before the armistice.
Military historian (born 1934) whose The Face of Battle (1976) shifted war history from commanders' strategies to the experience of ordinary soldiers.
Scottish historian (born 1964) whose The Pity of War (1998) controversially argued that Britain need not have entered the First World War in 1914.

items.title: WW1 — OverSimplified (Part 2)
items.description: Covers the later years of the war that shaped the revisionist debate — the Somme, disillusionment and armistice — giving context for competing historical interpretations of the conflict.

items.title: BBC Teach — YouTube Channel
items.description: BBC Teach's channel includes short curriculum clips on primary source analysis, Wilfred Owen and the poetry of the First World War, and how to evaluate historical evidence.

items.title: History Matters — YouTube Channel
items.description: Short-form animated Q&A videos that are excellent for understanding historiographical debates — why historians disagree, what revisionism means, and how interpretations change over time.

items.title: Oh! What a Lovely War (1969)
items.description: The film that cemented the 'lions led by donkeys' interpretation in popular culture — itself a valuable primary source for how the 1960s generation remembered and judged the First World War.

items.title: Gallipoli (1981)
items.description: Peter Weir's acclaimed film exploring the Gallipoli campaign from an Australian perspective, illustrating how Dominion nations developed their own distinct interpretations of the war.

items.title: Britannica: Historiography
items.description: Encyclopaedia Britannica's entry on historiography — the study of how historical knowledge is produced, why interpretations change, and the methods historians use to evaluate sources.

items.title: Britannica: Wilfred Owen
items.description: Britannica article on Wilfred Owen's life, the poems he wrote at Craiglockhart, and his influence on how the First World War has been remembered and interpreted.

items.title: The National Archives: The Great War 1914–1918
items.description: Source-based education resource using original documents to explore the First World War — ideal for practising source utility analysis with real primary evidence from the period.

items.title: IWM: First World War Recruitment Posters
items.description: IWM's dedicated page on WW1 recruitment posters — their content, provenance and the emotional appeals they made — an essential primary source for source utility questions.

items.title: The National Archives: General Haig — War Criminal or Great Commander?
items.description: Source-based enquiry using primary documents to examine competing interpretations of Haig's generalship — a direct example of how historians reach different conclusions from the same evidence.

items.title: The National Archives: Letters from the First World War, 1915
items.description: Primary source letters from soldiers and civilians, giving direct access to the kind of evidence historians use when building interpretations of the war's human experience.
